name: Kinesiology / face taping

lead: Face taping borrows elastic kinesiology tape from sports medicine and applies it to the face. Appearance-focused users hope it holds tissue lifted, retrains facial muscles and reduces puffiness for a more even, defined look.

Manufacturers have claimed the tape supports tissue, aids lymph drainage and improves proprioception. Reviews of the tape for musculoskeletal pain and strength report small or inconsistent effects, with some researchers attributing reported benefits to placebo. No study of cosmetic facial use was found; a registered trial compares physiotherapy and taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.

paras: Users cut strips of elastic tape and apply them along areas such as the cheeks, jaw or brow, often wearing them for periods during the day or overnight, sometimes alongside facial exercises.
Safety for facial use is not documented in the sources reviewed. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin.

chain: Tape lifts or holds facial tissue
angle.text: Users apply elastic sports tape to the face in the hope of holding tissue lifted, retraining facial muscles and reducing puffiness for a more even, defined look. The tape is studied for musculoskeletal use; facial use for appearance has not been tested.

lead: Kinesiology or face taping is the application of elastic therapeutic tape, of the kind developed for sports and musculoskeletal use, to the face. In appearance-focused communities it is used with the aim of looking more lifted and less puffy: people tape to hold facial tissue in a supported position, to retrain facial muscles, or to reduce puffiness and under-eye shadows.[1][2]

The idea is discussed in a looksmax.org thread titled as a question about whether face taping could be the next looksmax. The author argues that facial skin sags with gravity and sleep loss, and that gentle mechanical tension or compression from tape might change how skin and underlying fat behave. Commenters extend the idea to mouth taping, saying it could reduce lower-face bloat and under-eye circles.[2] These are community theories rather than findings.

Elastic kinesiology tape was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and is sold under the Kinesio brand among others.[1][3] It became widely visible after it was donated to athletes at the 2008 Beijing and 2012 London Olympics, and its use then spread from sport into everyday and cosmetic settings.[1] Manufacturers have claimed benefits for muscle support, lymphatic drainage, pain signalling and proprioception; published reviews in musculoskeletal conditions report small or inconsistent effects, and some researchers attribute reported benefits to placebo.[1] No published study has tested kinesiology tape for cosmetic facial purposes. A registered trial compares a physiotherapy technique with kinesiology taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.
infobox: Stretchy cotton with heat-activated acrylic adhesive[1]
Up to about four days (body use)[1]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a thin, stretchy, latex-free cotton strip that can stretch to roughly 140% of its length and bonds with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive. On the body it may be worn for several days.[1]

Wikipedia describes Kenzo Kase as the Japanese-American chiropractor who developed elastic therapeutic tape in the 1970s; the company he founded markets variants under the Kinesio brand and has acted against the word becoming a generic term.[1][3] The tape's public profile rose after it was donated to athletes at the 2008 Beijing Games, where beach volleyball player Kerri Walsh's visibly taped shoulder is credited with bringing it to a mass audience, and again at the 2012 London Games.[1] Science journalist Brian Dunning has suggested that sponsorship money may explain how often it appeared on televised athletes.[1]

Once the tape was familiar as a consumer product, people began applying it outside sport. Face taping belongs to this later wave: the same strips, cut and placed on the cheeks, jawline, forehead or around the eyes, with the goal of a lifted or less puffy look. The idea circulates mainly in looksmaxxing and skincare-adjacent discussion, where one looksmax.org thread framed it as a possible next appearance technique.[2] Mouth taping, a separate but often-mentioned practice, followed its own social media trend in the 2020s.[4]

Facial taping adapts the sports technique to the cheeks, jawline, forehead or around the eyes, with the aim of a lifted, smoother look. In the looksmax.org discussion, the author reasons that skin stretches downward with gravity during the day and recovers during sleep, and speculates that sustained stretch thins the fat layer while compression thickens it, citing a paper on mechanical regulation of adipose tissue volume.[2] A reply suggests the same logic could extend to the scalp and hair.[2]

A related practice is mouth taping, in which a strip of surgical tape holds the lips closed during sleep. Wikipedia reports that it became a social media trend in the 2020s, that its health claims have not been scientifically verified, and that small studies have examined snoring and sleep apnea; it does not describe facial appearance effects.[4] Forum users nonetheless claim it affects lower-face bloat and under-eye circles.[2]

Manufacturers state that the tape supports muscles, tendons, ligaments and joints, and further claims include improved lymphatic drainage, reduced pain signalling and better proprioception. Critics say these claims lack supporting evidence.[1]

A 2012 meta-analysis reported trivial pain relief and little quality evidence for the tape over other elastic taping in sports injuries. A 2014 meta-analysis reported negligible effects on muscle strength, with lower-quality studies more likely to report benefit. A 2015 meta-analysis found the tape outperformed no treatment for chronic musculoskeletal pain but not other treatments, and did not reduce disability. A 2018 study found tape colour, placement and tension did not measurably affect performance, strength or function. Some researchers attribute reported benefits to a placebo effect.[1] More recent trials and reviews continue to examine taping for ankle instability, shoulder pain and plantar fasciitis.[5][6]

A 2023 systematic review of nine randomised trials in chronic non-specific low back pain found that kinesiology tape reduced pain intensity immediately and at short-term follow-up, with no significant differences in disability, trunk range of motion, fear of movement or trunk muscle endurance compared with sham taping or with tape added to physiotherapy.[1]

Commentators including Reuters and the writer Steven Novella critiqued the evidence for the tape around the 2012 Olympics, and Science-Based Medicine did so again around the 2018 Winter Games, according to Wikipedia.[1] In 2017 KT Health settled a Massachusetts class action over unjust enrichment and misleading marketing, agreeing to pay $1.75 million and to refund half of the purchase price, which represented the premium over traditional athletic tape. The company dropped claims that the tape keeps users pain-free, prevents injury or gives 24-hour pain relief, and added the disclaimer 'not clinically proven for all injuries.'[1] The case concerned body use of the tape, not facial or cosmetic claims.
Safety of taping facial skin has not been studied. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin, and the Kinesio tape article describes the product as bonded with an acrylic adhesive.[1]

No studies found for cosmetic facial taping. One registered trial in Bell's palsy patients compares Kabat rehabilitation with kinesiology taping; it was listed as active, not recruiting, with 38 participants, and no results were reviewed. Studies of the tape in other body regions include a 2022 meta-analysis in athletes with chronic ankle instability and a randomised trial in plantar fasciitis.[5][6]

lore.intro: Face taping appears on looksmax.org as an experimental idea framed around gravity, sleep and skin tension, alongside mouth taping.[2]

claims.claim: Taping the face counters gravity-driven sagging and holds a lifted look.
Mouth taping reduces lower-face bloat and under-eye circles.
Sustained skin stretch or compression changes the fat layer under the skin.
Tape's lymph-drainage and proprioception effects can de-puff the face.

timeline.event: Kenzo Kase develops elastic kinesiology tape.[1][3]
Tape donated to athletes at the Beijing Olympics; Kerri Walsh's visible use is credited with mass exposure.[1]
Tape donated at the London Olympics; critics question the evidence.[1]
Meta-analyses report small or inconsistent effects in musculoskeletal conditions.[1]
KT Health settles a Massachusetts class action over marketing, paying $1.75 million.[1]
